verdict: Lend selectively to Anthurium growers tied to the Aizawl–Singapore export chain, structured on export receivables and crop-cycle cash flow; avoid diversified traders and loss-making floriculture peers.
title: Aizawl horticulture & floriculture: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Anthurium is a shade-grown cut flower that leaves Aizawl as a perishable consignment, not a commodity in a warehouse.** The first export was 1,024 cut flowers weighing 70 kg in 50 corrugated boxes, shipped by IVC Agrovet Pvt. Ltd. from Aizawl to Singapore via Kolkata [1][2]. Cash turns when the consignment clears and the buyer pays — so the working-capital cycle is short on inventory but long on receivables, and freight plus cold-chain handling sit between harvest and cash. **When a proposal lands, check the buyer name and the payment route first; if the buyer is not a named overseas importer, ask for the contract.**

## Where value and cash sit
**Value sits in the planting material and the post-harvest pack, not in the stem count.** The Zo Anthurium Growers Cooperative Society and the Department of Horticulture sit inside this chain [1], which tells you the grower base is organised but small-ticket. **Price realisation per stem, cost per stem and the Kolkata transit cost are not in our sources — collect from customer.** Peer floriculture economics are thin: Pushpanjali Floriculture's March 2026 net sales were Rs 13.18 crore, up 40.95% from Rs 9.35 crore, yet quarterly net loss was Rs 2.15 crore and EBITDA negative at Rs 0.24 crore [6]. **So when a proposal shows revenue growth with negative EBITDA, ask what the loss per stem is and who absorbs it.**

## What has changed
**The change is market access, not demand.** APEDA and the Mizoram Horticulture Department flagged off the first Anthurium consignment to Singapore [1][2][3]; these reports are from early 2025 and the APEDA piece is dated 24 Mar 2025 [1], so treat the export lane as proven once, not proven at scale. **Ask for the number of consignments shipped since that first one — collect from customer.** Our data pack gives no score for this industry or state [D], so the call rests on first principles and the peer set, not on a model output.

## Who to pursue, and how to grow safely
**Pursue the cooperative-linked Anthurium grower with a named Singapore buyer and a pack-house relationship; avoid the diversified agri-trader.** Nagarjuna Agri-Tech's revenue jumped from Rs 15.31 million to Rs 321.81 million year-on-year in the June 2026 quarter [5], with margin slipping to 7% as interest and depreciation rose [7] — that is trading turnover, not horticulture cash. **Structure on export receivables with a charge on the crop and the pack-house proceeds; take the consignment-wise shipment statement and the buyer payment advice every month.** Set a covenant that export receivables convert within the agreed transit-plus-credit period; if ageing crosses it, stop fresh disbursement.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch rejection rates and transit delays before you watch the P&L.** A perishable consignment rejected at Singapore is a total loss of that cycle, so a rising rejection count is the first signal. **Take monthly: consignment count, rejection count, realised price per stem, and receivable ageing.** If two consecutive months show falling consignment count with rising ageing, ask for the buyer's confirmation directly.
watch: Two months of falling shipments or any rejection -> freeze fresh disbursement and inspect the pack-house
Ageing beyond the agreed transit-plus-credit period -> stop limit renewal, seek buyer confirmation
Price falls while volumes hold -> re-cut the drawing power to actual realisations
Single buyer above half of shipments -> require a second named importer or reduce exposure
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
